newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Shotgun killer slays six in New Zealand hamlet.
newsitem.headline: Shotgun killer slays six in New Zealand hamlet.

text.p: A gunman went on a shooting rampage in a rural New Zealand hamlet on Saturday, killing six people and seriously wounding up to five others in another mass murder shattering the country's tranquil image.

A 24-year-old man had been charged with one count of murder, police said. They had found the suspect naked and unarmed in farmland close to the scene of the slayings in this small North Island town of Raurimu near the active volcano Mount Ruapehu.
An eerie silence enveloped the dozen farmhouses that make up Raurimu late on Saturday following the murders. There was little police presence and few signs of the early morning carnage.

Radio New Zealand quoted local residents as saying two of the victims were the parents of the alleged gunman and the other victims were related to him. They said he had a history of psychiatric problems.
Police would not confirm those reports but said earlier that the victims might have been related to the suspect.
Police said the suspect would appear in nearby Taumarunui District Court "in due course", and added other charges might be laid. His name was not released.

The gunman, using a 12-gauge shotgun, cut a swathe through Raurimu starting at the Spiral Lodge, used by skiers frequenting Mount Ruapehu's ski slopes in the peak winter season, and moving to another lodge, leaving bodies scattered over a wide area.
New Zealand is currently in mid-summer.
Police had earlier said there could be more victims but they later called off the search.
Wanganui Acting District Commander Jeff Holloway said police took the suspect into custody shortly before midday (2300 GMT).
The murders were committed around 9.00 a.m. on Saturday (2000 GMT Friday).

"The victims have not yet been properly identified. We don't know all the names as yet. We believe that a number of them at least are residents and may be related to the suspect," he told a news conference.
The wounded were ferried by helicopters to hospitals in the district, he said.
Helicopter pilot Guy Beange described the scene as "like Vietnam", with police and helicopters everywhere.
Saturday's slaying is the fifth mass slaughter in the 1990s that has shocked the country and undermined its image as a green and peaceful place.
In 1990, 13 people were killed by a young man in the hamlet of Aromana, near Dunedin in the south of the South Island. The police shot the gunman David Gray dead after a siege.
In May, 1992, 64-year-old farmer Brian Schlaepfer shot or stabbed six members of his family before killing himself with a shotgun at Pukekohe, near the northern city of Auckland.
The following month, an unemployed 25-year-old man stabbed or bludgeoned to death seven relatives including five children in the quiet rural town of Masterton, north of Wellington.

Then in 1994 a family of two parents and three children were shot dead with a rifle. Son David Bain was convicted for the mass murders but protested his innocence contending the father carried out the murders before committing suicide.
The series of massacres have traumatised New Zealand's 3.5 million people who used to take pride in the relatively low rate of violence. Violent crime has been on the increase for a number of years.
After the Aramona massacre, the government moved to tighten gunlaws and prohibit the sale of military-style assault rifles, which had been freely available.

But the laws did not come under the kind of scrutiny witnessed in Australia after the Port Arthur massacre of 35 people or in Britain after the Dunblane killing of 16 children and their teacher, both last year.
"Why must we always wait for yet another gun massacre before we tighten our firearms laws," said gun policy lobbyist Philip Alpers.
He said New Zealand had one gun for every household, 11 times as many as in Britain and 60 percent more than Australia.
